issues.legal_issue: A revisional authority cannot take over the statutory functions of the lower authority by deciding individual applications directly or directing the lower authority how to decide them.
material_facts: The governing statute made the development authority responsible for considering allotment applications and gave the State Government revisional power over orders already made by that authority.
The development authority had not decided the applicants’ allotment claims before the State Government considered them.
The State Government directly considered the claims and directed the development authority to make allotments, without giving the affected parties an opportunity to be heard.
issues.conclusion: The State Government had no occasion to entertain the applications directly or direct allotments. Its orders were an improper exercise of statutory power and were vitiated.
issues.legal_principle: Under Section 41(1) of the U.P. Urban Planning and Development Act, 1973, the State Government may issue directions for efficient administration of the Act; Section 41(3) confers revisional power to examine the legality or propriety of an order or direction already made by the authority. These powers do not permit the State Government to decide individual applications assigned to the statutory authority or to substitute its judgment for that authority’s. The Court relied on Rakesh Ranjan Verma v. State of Bihar, U.P. State Electricity Board v. Ram Autar, Bangalore Development Authority v. R. Hanumaiah, Bangalore Medical Trust v. B.S. Muddappa, Poonam Verma v. Delhi Development Authority, Chandrika Jha v. State of Bihar, Anirudhsinhji Karansinghji Jadeja v. State of Gujarat, and other cited authorities concerning the exercise of statutory discretion.

predicates.statutory_revision_proceeding: The proceeding concerns a superior authority exercising a statutory revisional role over a lower statutory body.
predicates.no_lower_authority_order_under_review: The lower statutory body has not made an order on the matter for the superior authority to review.
predicates.superior_authority_decides_individual_ap: The superior authority itself considers and decides an individual application assigned by law to the lower statutory body.
predicates.superior_authority_directs_individual_ou: The superior authority directs the lower statutory body to reach a specified outcome on an individual application.

issues.definition: When a superior authority in a statutory revision proceeding decides an individual matter without an underlying order, or dictates its outcome to the lower body, the superior authority’s action is without authority.

issues.legal_issue: An action taken in knowing defiance of a court’s subsisting interim restraint is ineffective and cannot be enforced.
material_facts: An interim High Court order restrained the authorities from allotting the disputed land to anyone else.
The State Government and the development authority knew that the interim order remained in force.
Despite that restraint, the State Government directed an allotment and the development authority issued an allotment letter.
issues.conclusion: The allotment action taken in contravention of the interim order remained a nullity and was unenforceable.
issues.legal_principle: An act done in disobedience of a court order is illegal and may be treated as not having taken place for the purposes of the proceedings. The Court relied on Mulraj v. Murti Raghunathji Maharaj, Surjit Singh v. Harbans Singh, All Bengal Excise Licensees Association v. Raghabendra Singh, Delhi Development Authority v. Skipper Construction Co., and Gurunath Manohar Pavaskar v. Nagesh Siddappa Navalgund.

rule.if: court_proceeding_with_interim_restraint and action_taken_while_restraint_in_force and decision_maker_knew_of_restraint and action_conflicted_with_restraint

predicates.court_proceeding_with_interim_restraint: A court proceeding includes an interim order restraining specified conduct.
predicates.action_taken_while_restraint_in_force: An authority takes the relevant action while the interim restraint remains in force.
predicates.decision_maker_knew_of_restraint: The decision-maker knew that the interim restraint remained in force.
predicates.action_conflicted_with_restraint: The action taken is contrary to what the interim order restrains.

issues.definition: An authority’s action is null and unenforceable when it is taken during a court-imposed restraint, with knowledge of that restraint, and in conflict with it.

issues.legal_issue: A court cannot grant a party substantive relief that the party did not request.
material_facts: The writ petition sought to quash an allotment made in favour of another person.
The petitioner did not seek an order directing that the land be allotted to him.
The High Court nevertheless directed that the land be allotted to the petitioner.
issues.conclusion: The High Court was not permitted to direct an allotment that the petitioner had not sought.
issues.legal_principle: A case must be decided on the pleadings, and a court cannot grant relief that was not claimed, particularly without an amendment setting out the basis for that relief. The Court relied on Messrs. Trojan & Co. v. R.M.N.N. Nagappa Chettiar, Krishna Priya Ganguly v. University of Lucknow, Om Prakash v. Ram Kumar, Bharat Amratlal Kothari v. Dosukhan Samadkhan Sindhi, and Fertilizer Corporation of India v. Sarat Chandra Rath.

predicates.court_proceeding_on_party_claim: A court is deciding a proceeding in which a party has specified the relief it seeks.
predicates.granted_relief_not_requested: The court grants substantive relief that the party did not request.

issues.definition: When a court deciding a party’s claim grants substantive relief beyond what that party requested, it cannot grant that relief.

issues.legal_issue: The land policy did not permit allotment benefits for land acquired for roads or allotment of sites in a commercial area where the policy provided for residential sites.
material_facts: The land policy provided for allotment of developed land in a residential area to qualifying owners whose land had been acquired, except for land covered by roads.
The land claimed by one applicant had been acquired for roads.
The sites allotted to both applicants were in a commercial area, while the policy provided only for residential-area allotments.
issues.conclusion: The applicant whose land had been acquired for roads could not claim the policy benefit, and the allotments in the commercial area were contrary to the policy and illegal.
issues.legal_principle: The Court applied the terms of the land policy, which limited the benefit to residential-area land and excluded land covered by roads. It also noted that the policy had not been declared invalid or contrary to the equality guarantee in Article 14 of the Constitution.

predicates.land_policy_allotment_claim: A person seeks an allotment benefit under a policy for owners whose land was acquired.
predicates.acquired_land_reserved_for_roads: The land for which the claimant seeks the benefit was acquired for roads.
predicates.proposed_site_is_commercial: The site proposed for allotment is in a commercial area rather than a residential area.

issues.definition: A claimant cannot receive the policy allotment benefit when the acquired land was for roads or the proposed allotment site is commercial.

issues.legal_issue: A claimant seeking a benefit dependent on a timely application must establish that the application was made within the required time, and an authority’s decision does not by itself establish condonation of delay.
material_facts: The claimant asserted that an application for the policy benefit had been filed in time, but the record of receipt contained suspicious features, including a last entry in a register and a receiving clerk’s signature by a person who joined service later.
The claimant did not establish how the application had been sent or produce supporting postal evidence.
The High Court treated the State Government’s consideration of the claim as implicitly condoning any delay without examining whether there was sufficient cause.
issues.conclusion: The claimant had to establish timely filing, and the suspicious and unsupported record did not permit the application to be entertained; the State Government’s consideration of the claim did not amount to deemed condonation of delay.
issues.legal_principle: The burden of establishing an asserted fact lies on the person who alleges it. Where an application is late, the authority must consider whether it has power to condone delay and whether sufficient cause prevented timely filing. Delay cannot be treated as condoned merely because an authority considered the application, particularly where the delay was not considered with application of mind.

rule.if: claim_for_time_limited_benefit and timely_filing_not_established and (receipt_record_is_suspicious or supporting_proof_of_filing_is_absent)

predicates.claim_for_time_limited_benefit: A claimant seeks a benefit that requires an application within a prescribed time.
predicates.timely_filing_not_established: The claimant has not established that the application was filed within the required time.
predicates.receipt_record_is_suspicious: The record relied on to show receipt of the application has circumstances casting doubt on its authenticity or timing.
predicates.supporting_proof_of_filing_is_absent: The claimant has not produced supporting evidence showing how or when the application was sent or received.

issues.definition: A time-limited benefit application cannot be treated as timely when the claimant has not established timely filing and the receipt record is suspicious or lacks supporting proof.

issues.legal_issue: A party seeking discretionary writ relief must make a full and truthful disclosure of material facts and may be denied relief for withholding facts that mislead the court.
material_facts: The allotment to the private appellant was made for land in a commercial area, although the policy provided for residential-area land.
The private appellant did not disclose to the Court that the allotted land was in a commercial area.
The Court found that the appellant had not approached it with the true facts.
issues.conclusion: The appellant had not approached the Court with full disclosure of the true facts, and the Court treated the conduct as an abuse of the judicial process.
issues.legal_principle: Relief under Articles 226 and 227 of the Constitution is discretionary and equitable. A litigant must disclose material facts fully and truthfully, and a court may refuse relief where its process is abused or it is misled. The Court relied on The Ramjas Foundation v. Union of India, K.P. Srinivas v. R.M. Premchand, Nooruddin v. K.L. Anand, Ramniklal N. Bhutta v. State of Maharashtra, Abdul Rahman v. Prasony Bai, S.J.S. Business Enterprises v. State of Bihar, and Oswal Fats & Oils Ltd. v. Additional Commissioner.

predicates.extraordinary_writ_proceeding: The proceeding asks a court to exercise extraordinary writ jurisdiction.
predicates.claimant_seeks_discretionary_relief: The claimant seeks relief that depends on the court’s discretion.
predicates.material_fact_withheld_from_court: The claimant does not disclose a material fact relevant to the relief sought.

issues.definition: A court may refuse discretionary relief in an extraordinary writ proceeding when the claimant withholds a material fact.
